title: What does better context cost?
text:
Costs and value / Example inputs
We want to know the cost of doing a task well. Finding the right facts is one part of that cost. We have not measured gains in work output, what users would pay, or savings in a real firm.

title: What does better context cost?
text:
What costs should we count?
\[C_{\mathrm{task}}=C_{\mathrm{inference}}+C_{\mathrm{memory}}+C_{\mathrm{storage}}+wT_{\mathrm{active}}+C_{\mathrm{errors}}.\]
A memory tool must extract, store, find, rank, and sum up text. Count the cost of each step. Spread setup costs across a stated number of uses. Track hands-on work time apart from time spent waiting for the model. Do not count the same fix as both time spent and an error cost. Cached text, which a system stores for reuse, may have a different price.

title: What does better context cost?
text:
The cost of input text

costs <- expand.grid(input_tokens=c(8000,32000,128000,512000),price_per_million=c(.1,.5,1,3,10)) |>
  mutate(cost=input_tokens*price_per_million/1e6)
ggplot(costs,aes(factor(input_tokens/1000),factor(price_per_million),fill=cost)) +
  geom_tile(colour='white') + geom_text(aes(label=sprintf('$%.3f',cost)),size=3.4) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='#edf5f7',high='#67aaa8') +
  labs(x='Input tokens (thousands)',y='Assumed USD per million input tokens',fill='USD',
       title='Input cost increases with context length and unit price',
       subtitle='Example costs; excludes cached rates, output, and memory tools')








The chart uses example prices and token counts. It does not turn our word counts into billed tokens. A token is a unit of text that a model reads or writes. See the price page for the listed base prices in our sample.

title: What does better context cost?
section: How much time would it need to save?
text:
How much time would it need to save?

# Example inputs. We have not measured time saved or returns.
scenario <- expand.grid(tasks=c(20,100,500),minutes_saved=seq(0,5,.1)) |>
  mutate(net_value=tasks*minutes_saved/60*30 - 20 - tasks*.02)
ggplot(scenario,aes(minutes_saved,net_value,colour=factor(tasks))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept=0,linetype='dashed') + geom_line(linewidth=1) +
  labs(x='Assumed work minutes saved per task',y='Monthly value after costs (USD, example)',
       colour='Tasks / month',title='The value depends on how much work time it saves',
       subtitle='Assumptions: $30/hour, $20/month fixed cost, $0.02 extra cost/task')








We assume time is worth $30 per hour. We also assume a $20 monthly fee and $0.02 extra cost per task. These are example inputs, not measured market rates. We still need to measure time saved with real users and matched tasks.

title: What does better context cost?
text:
Try your own inputs
Tasks / monthWork minutes saved / taskValue of work time ($/hour)Fixed cost / month ($)Extra AI cost / task ($)

The tool values time saved, then subtracts fixed and per-task costs. It leaves out error costs. It assumes each saved minute has the value you set. That value may not turn into cash savings. Change the inputs to see when the result changes.

title: What does better context cost?
text:
The cost of switching tools
Moving to a new AI tool can take time. Users may need to bring their project notes and past decisions with them. A tool that lets them move this context could reduce that burden. Access rules, file formats, and upkeep could limit the gain. OECD research on data portability explores this wider issue. Our study has not measured the effect of our tool on switching costs.

title: What does better context cost?
section: How to test the business case
text:
How to test the business case
First, choose what to compare the tool with. Check work quality before putting a price on time saved. Count setup and upkeep costs. Show where the tool fails as well as where it helps. In a later test, assign matched tasks to each workflow at random. Measure time spent on setup and fixes. Have graders score the work without knowing which tool produced it. A small survey can describe users’ views. It cannot prove that the tool saves money.

title: AI model prices and context limits
text:
Our analysis · R + SQL · One point in time
We use 304 model listings from 12 developers. OpenRouter lists the base price to route text to each model. We show dollars per million tokens. A token is a unit of text a model reads or writes. These prices do not show sales, usage, or chat subscription fees. Source and price fields.

title: AI model prices and context limits
section: How context size and price are linked
text:
How context size and price are linked
To study prices, we fit a regression. It links context size to output price. It also accounts for who makes the model and whether it reads images. The equation is:
\[\log(p_j)=\alpha+\beta\log(c_j)+\gamma_{developer(j)}+\delta\,image_j+\epsilon_j.\]
The fit uses 283 model versions. The context coefficient is 0.171, and R² is 0.382. R² measures the share of variation in log prices that the fit explains in this sample. At twice the context size, the fitted output price differs by about 12.6%. This holds the developer and image support fixed.
This fit does not show cause and effect. It does not tell us how buyers would react to a price change. More context does not prove better quality. We lack matched scores over time, demand, and the cost of running each model. We also lack price changes driven by outside events. Model families and firms may share errors. We do not treat each listing as an independent sample for tests of significance.

catalog <- jsonlite::fromJSON('data/processed/analysis_sample.json')
fit <- lm(log(output_price) ~ log(context_tokens) + factor(company) + image_input,
          data = catalog)
coef(fit)["log(context_tokens)"]

log(context_tokens) 
          0.1705679 



library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

theme_set(

    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#102824"),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#53635f"),
      axis.title = element_text(color = "#53635f"),
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#fcfbf7", color = NA)
    )
)

ggplot(catalog, aes(context_tokens, output_price, color = company)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .65, size = 2) +

  scale_y_log10() +

    title = "Context size is one of many model traits",

Questions, chat sessions, messages, and test runs are different counts. LoCoMo has ten chat histories that many questions share. LongMemEval gives each question a history, but some histories reuse the same sessions. A repeated session is not a new source. These files mix chats made for tests with other shared text. They do not form a sample of our users or of all workers.

title: The data behind the study
text:
What do the questions test?

task_counts <- q |> count(dataset, category)
ggplot(task_counts, aes(n, reorder(category, n), fill=dataset)) +
  geom_col(show.legend=FALSE) + facet_wrap(~dataset, scales='free_y') +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c('#287d70','#39769c')) +
  labs(x='Questions', y=NULL, title='The two test sets ask different kinds of questions')








We leave questions with no answer out of the recall scores. This includes the adversarial tests, which ask about facts the history cannot supply. We keep them in the data counts. We also leave out questions with missing source labels or labels we cannot match. The download lists each reason. A later test should check whether an AI knows when to say it does not know.

title: The data behind the study
section: How long are the chat histories?
text:
How long are the chat histories?

ggplot(h, aes(words, colour=dataset)) + stat_ecdf(linewidth=1) +
  scale_x_log10(labels=scales::comma) + scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent) +
  labs(x='Words in a chat history (log scale)', y='Share at or below this length',
       colour=NULL, title='LongMemEval gives each question more text to search',
       subtitle='LoCoMo: 10 conversations; LongMemEval-S: 500 question histories')








We count words split by spaces, including names, roles, and dates. Words are not the same as tokens, the text units an AI model reads. In this chart, LoCoMo adds one record per chat history. LongMemEval adds one per question history.

title: The data behind the study
text:
Where are the key facts?

ggplot(filter(q, eligible), aes(earliest_evidence, fill=dataset)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth=.1, boundary=0, colour='white', show.legend=FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~dataset, scales='free_y') + scale_x_continuous(labels=scales::percent) +
  labs(x='Position of the first marked source session', y='Questions we scored',
       title='Key facts can sit far back in the chat history')








We place each session at the midpoint of its slot in the history. We then divide that position by the number of sessions. The scale runs from the start of the history to the end. A method that keeps the latest sessions can miss older facts. This chart shows where facts sit in the data. It does not show where an AI pays attention.

title: The data behind the study
section: How many sessions does a question need?
text:
How many sessions does a question need?

burden <- filter(q, eligible) |> count(dataset, gold_sessions) |>
  group_by(dataset) |> mutate(share=n/sum(n))
ggplot(burden, aes(factor(gold_sessions), share, fill=dataset)) +
  geom_col(show.legend=FALSE) + facet_wrap(~dataset, scales='free_x') +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent) +
  labs(x='Number of marked source sessions needed', y='Share of questions we scored',
       title='Some questions need facts from several sessions')








Some questions need facts from more than one session. We show the mean share of marked sessions each method finds. We also show how often it finds them all. Other sessions may hold the same facts without a label. Our scores use the labels the source gives us.

title: Context Management Across AI Tools: Memory, Reliability, and Cost
text:
Independent Research Project




Memory, Reliability, and Cost
What should an AI tool remember? We test how tools can find the right facts, how much context they need, and what it costs to keep it.
See the experiment Explore the datasets

title: Context Management Across AI Tools: Memory, Reliability, and Cost
text:
The question we test
Which way of choosing context finds the most useful facts? We test three methods: BM25 keyword search, keeping the latest chats, and a random choice. We set four limits on how many chat sessions each method can keep. These simple methods give us a starting point for testing the tool.


01 / The data

What needs to stay?


See the types of questions, the size of each chat history, and where the key facts sit.

View the data →


02 / Our test

Which facts do we find?


Compare the three methods. See how scores change across tasks and chat histories.

Read the results →


03 / Costs and value

What could it save?


Explore costs, time saved, and the point at which the tool could pay for itself.

Explore the costs →

title: Context Management Across AI Tools: Memory, Reliability, and Cost
text:
What we found
At a limit of five sessions, BM25 raises mean evidence recall by 63.8 percentage points on LoCoMo and 77.6 points on LongMemEval-S. Both gains use the latest-chat method as the base. Recall is the share of source sessions with key facts that a method finds. We score both methods on the same set of questions. These gains do not show how well an AI would answer or how much time a person would save.

ggplot(curves, aes(k, recall, colour=strategy)) +
  geom_line(linewidth=1) + geom_point(size=2.5) + facet_wrap(~dataset) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=palette) + scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(1,3,5,10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent, limits=c(0,1)) +
  labs(x='Session limit', y='Mean recall of marked source sessions', colour=NULL,
       title='The method changes which source sessions we find',
       subtitle='Our search test measures source recall, not answer quality')








How we ran the tests · Download all test scores

title: Context Management Across AI Tools: Memory, Reliability, and Cost
section: What this means for the platform
text:
What this means for the platform
A memory tool should keep links to its source text. It should track which facts are current and keep projects apart. This test checks how we find text. We still need to test conflicting facts, moves between tools, ease of use, and the answers an AI gives.

title: How we choose which context to keep
text:
Our test / Finding facts in past chats
We ran 24,072 tests on 2,006 questions with usable source labels. Each test combines a question, a method, and a session limit. Each method sees the same question and chat history. We use the answer and source labels to score the chosen sessions, not to choose them. We made no calls to an AI model.

title: How we choose which context to keep
text:
Three methods, four session limits








Method
How it chooses sessions
Why we include it




BM25
Finds query words, gives more weight to rare words, and adjusts for session length
A simple keyword search


Recent
Keeps the latest sessions first
A common way to trim a chat history


Random
Shuffles the sessions with a fixed seed
A chance-based reference we can repeat



Each method can keep up to 1, 3, 5, or 10 sessions. Sessions vary in length. The same count can mean a different number of words, tokens, and dollars. We search text and skip images. See the test settings for the full rules and the random seed.

title: How we choose which context to keep
text:
Evidence recall

ggplot(curves, aes(k, recall, colour=strategy)) +
  geom_line(linewidth=1) + geom_point(size=2.5) + facet_wrap(~dataset) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=palette) + scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(1,3,5,10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent, limits=c(0,1)) +
  labs(x='Session limit', y='Mean recall of marked source sessions', colour=NULL,
       title='The method changes which source sessions we find',
       subtitle='Our search test measures source recall, not answer quality')








Recall is the share of a question’s marked source sessions that a method finds. A score of 100% means it found all of them. It does not mean an AI read those facts well or gave the right answer.

title: How we choose which context to keep
text:
Finding all the facts

ggplot(curves, aes(k, all_hit, colour=strategy)) +
  geom_line(linewidth=1) + geom_point(size=2.5) + facet_wrap(~dataset) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=palette) + scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(1,3,5,10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent, limits=c(0,1)) +
  labs(x='Session limit', y='Share of questions with all marked sources found',
       colour=NULL, title='Finding some sources is easier than finding them all')








Finding some facts may not be enough. A task that spans several sessions may need them all. A tool should flag when it lacks part of the source text.

title: How we choose which context to keep
text:
Scores by task

ggplot(cats, aes(strategy, category, fill=recall)) +
  geom_tile(colour='white') + geom_text(aes(label=sprintf('%.0f%%',100*recall)),size=3.2) +
  facet_wrap(~dataset, scales='free_y') +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='#f0f3f7',high='#63b9a5',limits=c(0,1),labels=scales::percent) +
  labs(x=NULL,y=NULL,fill='Recall',title='Scores vary by the type of question',
       subtitle='Recall at a five-session limit; task counts are in the download')








Some task groups have more questions than others. Read the scores with their counts. Download the scores and counts by task.

For LoCoMo, we draw from the ten chat histories 2,000 times, with replacement. Each draw keeps the questions from a history together. We then find the mean score gain, giving each question the same weight. The middle 95% of these gains forms a cluster-bootstrap interval. This shows how the gain varies when we change the mix of histories. Ten histories give a limited view of that range. We cannot treat it as a precise range for all users. LongMemEval reuses source text across histories. We show its score gain without an interval that assumes each question is independent.

# Executed in R/context_analysis.R; paired differences are clustered by conversation.
set.seed(20261001)
x <- subset(clusters, dataset == 'LoCoMo')
boot <- replicate(2000, {
  sampled <- sample(seq_len(nrow(x)), replace = TRUE)
  sum(x$total[sampled]) / sum(x$n[sampled])
})
quantile(boot, c(.025, .975))


ggplot(filter(clusters,dataset=='LoCoMo'), aes(reorder(cluster,gain),100*gain)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept=0,colour='#8797a1') + geom_segment(aes(xend=cluster,y=0,yend=100*gain),colour='#287d70') +
  geom_point(size=3,colour='#287d70') + coord_flip() +
  labs(x='Conversation',y='BM25 minus Recent (percentage points)',
       title='Score gains in each of the ten chat histories',
       subtitle='Each point shows the mean gain at a five-session limit')

section: How much text do we need to keep?
text:
How much text do we need to keep?

       title='Keeping less text can mean losing key facts',subtitle='Point labels show session limits; words are not billed tokens')








Keeping less text can mean losing key facts. This chart compares the share of words kept with recall. It does not measure answer quality or cost in dollars. We choose whole sessions, and their lengths vary.

title: What published tests show
text:
Published scores / Our analysis
We use a saved version of the RULER score table. It has 264 scores for 45 model versions. Other researchers ran these tests. The table gives combined scores, not each trial or monthly results. It includes older models and scores from outside teams. Their test details can differ.

title: What published tests show
section: What happens as the input grows?
text:
What happens as the input grows?

order_models <- rr |> group_by(model) |> summarise(avg=mean(score)) |> arrange(avg) |> pull(model)
ggplot(rr,aes(factor(tested_tokens/1000),factor(model,levels=order_models),fill=score)) +
  geom_tile(colour='white') + geom_text(aes(label=sprintf('%.0f',score)),size=2.8) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low='#f9eadc',high='#469d9b',limits=c(0,100)) +
  labs(x='Test length (thousands of tokens)',y=NULL,fill='Score',
       title='Published RULER scores across context lengths',
       subtitle='Scores from older models; this is not a ranking of current tools')








Some tests use more text than a model claims to support. The first chart keeps those scores. The comparisons below use lengths within each claimed limit. Stars in the source mark scores from outside teams. Our data file keeps that flag. We leave missing scores blank. We keep the source labels 4K–128K; these are length labels, not exact counts from each model’s tokenizer.

title: What published tests show
section: Compare each model at two lengths
text:
Compare each model at two lengths

ggplot(drops,aes(reorder(model,drop),drop)) +
  geom_col(fill='#39769c',width=.7) + coord_flip() +
  labs(x=NULL,y='Score at 4K minus score at 128K (points)',
       title='Scores can fall as the input grows',
       subtitle='Published scores; each model claims to support at least 128K')








We compare 34 models with scores at both lengths and a claimed limit of at least 128K. The median drop is 18.1 points. The median is the middle value when we sort the drops. These are older model tests. They do not predict how current tools will score.
We also fit a regression with model fixed effects. This lets each model have its own starting score. Within the claimed limits, the fit links each doubling of length to a -4.33 point score change. This is a pattern in the table, not proof that length caused the change. We lack scores for each trial, so we report no trial-level standard errors or p-values.

ruler_fit <- lm(score ~ log2(tested_tokens / 4000) + factor(model),
                data = subset(rr, !beyond_claim))
coef(ruler_fit)[2]

log2(tested_tokens/4000) 
               -4.334504 



selected <- c('Gemini-1.5-pro','GPT-4-1106-preview','Qwen3-14B (14B)','Llama3.1 (70B)')
ggplot(filter(rr,model %in% selected),aes(tested_tokens/1000,score,colour=model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth=1) + geom_point(size=2) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks=c(4,8,16,32,64,128)) +
  labs(x='Test length (thousands of tokens, log scale)',y='Published RULER score',colour=NULL,
       title='Four older models show different score drops')








These four models show different score patterns. We did not choose them as the top four. The first chart shows the full set.

title: Methods and sources
text:
Run the study
Open AI-Economy.Rproj in RStudio. From the project directory:
python3 scripts/fetch_benchmarks.py
python3 scripts/evaluate_retrieval.py
Rscript R/context_analysis.R
python3 scripts/audit_results.py
quarto render
quarto preview
To rebuild the model price data, run scripts/prepare_data.py, then R/analyze.R. Install these R packages: jsonlite, dplyr, ggplot2, scales, knitr, and rmarkdown. The Python code needs no extra packages. You need no model API key or paid calls. The project ZIP leaves out the large LongMemEval raw file. The download script fetches the saved source version. It checks a SHA-256 hash, a file fingerprint, to confirm the file matches.
Each graph has the R code that made it above it. context_setup.R loads the data and sets the style. context_figures.R holds the graph code. We also save the R version and package details.

title: Methods and sources
text:
How the search test works
We treat a whole chat session as one document. It includes the date, roles, and text. For LoCoMo, we map each labeled source turn to its session. For LongMemEval, we use the source-session IDs in the release. Each search uses the given question. It cannot see the answer, source labels, source summaries, or has_answer flags.
BM25 splits text into lowercase words and numbers. It removes a fixed list of common words and does not shorten words to their stems. Its settings are k1 = 1.5 and b = 0.75. Tied scores keep the order of the source sessions, from oldest to newest. The Recent method reverses that order. Random uses a seed from the question ID and dataset name, hashed with SHA-256. The same inputs give the same shuffle. We keep up to 1, 3, 5, or 10 sessions, capped by how many exist. The random score comes from one shuffle per question. It is not the mean of all possible shuffles.
We leave no-answer and adversarial questions out of recall scoring. We also leave out questions whose source labels are missing or do not match. We keep all of them in the data counts. Recall needs a known set of source sessions to find. This choice means we do not test whether an AI knows when to decline an answer. We skip images. Finding a whole source session also does not prove an AI will use the right line.
Full test settings · Questions left out · Data counts

title: Methods and sources
text:
How to read the statistics
Our main comparison is BM25 minus Recent at a five-session limit. We compare scores on the same questions. We set this plan before we looked at the scores. We did not register it with an outside service. Other limits, task groups, and source positions help us explore the results. We report the size of each gap. We do not run a long list of tests and pick those with small p-values.
LoCoMo questions share ten chat histories. For the bootstrap, we draw whole histories with replacement. This keeps linked questions together. With just ten histories, the range gives a limited view of how the result may vary. LongMemEval histories also share source text. We show its fixed test-set gap without a confidence interval that assumes each question is independent. Neither set is a random sample of real users.
Messages, tokens, scores, and repeated tests do not count distinct users. RULER gives combined scores, not the trial-level data we would need to estimate sampling error. The model fixed effects describe score patterns. They do not prove effects on jobs, pay, or work output.

title: Methods and sources
text:
How we check the data
We record the exact Git or Hugging Face version of each raw file. We also record its SHA-256 hash. We leave missing scores blank. The source file list gives file names, sizes, download times, and links. We log questions left out of scoring. We do not give them zero recall when their labels are missing.
We found 13 LongMemEval histories with one repeated session ID each. Each pair has the same message text. None is a marked source session. We keep these repeats so the test sees the file as released. A repeat is not a new source session. We report total appearances and distinct IDs as separate counts. We do not turn one snapshot into a made-up history.

title: Methods and sources
text:
Monthly data: a next step
We have not collected monthly data from AI firms. A future study could track prices, context limits, and scores on a fixed test set. A list of model launch dates would not supply monthly test scores. We would also need to keep tests of new model versions apart from repeat tests of the same version.

title: Methods and sources
section: What we still need to test
text:
What we still need to test
This study tests the search step. It does not test syncing across tools, vector search, summaries, conflicting facts, or final answers. Next, we should use fixed model versions on the same tasks. We should match context budgets and compare with full-history input. Graders should not know which method produced each answer. We should measure all costs. We have not run those tests yet.

title: Methods and sources
section: How we will use survey answers
text:
How we will use survey answers
The survey asks one main question: how often do recent AI users repeat context? Count recent users who answer “Yes” to question 4. Divide that count by recent users who answer “Yes” or “No” to that question. Report both counts with the percent. Leave missing, unsure, and conflicting answers out of that base count, and report them apart. Time spent and tool choice add context. They are not extra tests of the main claim.
A first survey of 30–60 people could help us test the form. It would not speak for all workers. A Wilson interval gives a range for a share under a model of independent responses. It does not fix bias in who joins the survey, duplicate answers, or errors in recall. Do not claim a margin of error for all workers.

# Run only after real responses are collected and screened.
# x = recent users who re-entered context; n = recent users with a Yes/No answer.
wilson <- function(x, n, confidence = 0.95) {
  stopifnot(n > 0, x >= 0, x <= n, x == floor(x), n == floor(n))
  z <- qnorm(1 - (1 - confidence) / 2)
  p <- x / n
  center <- (p + z^2 / (2*n)) / (1 + z^2/n)
  half <- z * sqrt(p*(1-p)/n + z^2/(4*n^2)) / (1 + z^2/n)
  c(proportion=p, lower=center-half, upper=center+half)
}


Set up the survey
Download the Google Forms script. Paste it into a new Google Apps Script project and run createPulseForm. The log shows the edit and response links. The script makes a six-question form and a response sheet. It routes people who do not consent to the end. We have not run it in your account. Check who can view and answer the form before you share it.
